awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: Vacuum Stripping and Absorption (VaSA) to Recover Wastewater Ammonia and Treat Digestate
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Technology Transfer Phase I project is advancing efficiency of wastewater infrastructure by filling the gap of scalable technologies to cost-effectively recover ammonia in wastewater. Nitrogen is one of the primary nutrients that are essential for the normal growth of plants. Nitrogen in the fertilizers applied for food production ends up largely in wastewater. This project is to translate the innovative Vacuum Stripping and Absorption (VaSA) process into a cost-effective, scalable technology for recovery of ammonia in wastewater while upgrading the biosolids in the treated wastewater and increasing production of renewable natural gas. The proposed technology promotes efficiency by turning wastewater pollutants like ammonia into high-purity nitrogen fertilizers. It holds a great promise to substantially reduce the operational costs for water resource recovery facilities and concentrated animal feeding operations to meet regulatory requirements for discharge of treated wastewater and land application of animal manure. The recovered fertilizers and upgraded biosolids generate revenues for the facilities and operations.  

The VaSA process brings wastewater to boiling under vacuum at a temperature much below the normal boiling point, under which ammonia is effectively stripped out of wastewater, separated from water vapor in a demister, and absorbed to an acidic solution to form ammonium sulfate crystals. Through pilot tests using a 3-pool VaSA prototype, this project will for the first time explore the regulation of vapor-liquid equilibrium profile from the complex boiling wastewater to the water-ammonia binary system in the stripper head and demister. When scaling up the VaSA technology, vapor-liquid equilibrium evolves from the multi-pool boiling stripper throughout the demister and varies with the number of vertically mounted pools and demister configuration. Understanding the vapor-liquid equilibrium profile will derisk the multi-pool scaling-up design approach and inline production of solid fertilizers. By controlling the factors that regulate vapor-liquid equilibrium, the technology can be scaled up for continuous operation without compromise of its high efficiency for ammonia recovery while maintaining minimal energy consumption. Moreover, it is expected to prove the high efficiency of anaerobic digestion under alkaline conditions and elucidate the mechanisms of alkaline anaerobic digestion through laboratory digestion experiments coupled with a single-pool VaSA prototype.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Nitrogen is one of the primary plant nutrients. Nitrogen applied in food production ends up in liquid wastes such as biosolids at wastewater treatment plants and animal manure at concentrated animal feeding operations. Cost-effective removal of ammonia from wastewater has been a great challenge. The goal of this Small Business Technology Transfer Phase I project was to develop the novel Vacuum Stripping and Absorption (VaSA) process into a cost-saving, scalable technology for efficient treatment of liquid wastes and recovery of ammonia in waste streams. The VaSA process brings liquid wastes to boiling under vacuum at a temperature much lower than the normal boiling point, under which ammonia is efficiently stripped out of waste, separated from water vapor in a demister, and absorbed to an acid solution to form ammonium sulfate crystals. Vacuum stripping also substantially reduces pathogens, thus upgrading biosolids from Class B to more valuable Class A and safeguarding the use of dewatered manure solids for animal bedding and land application.

The first objective of this project was to derisk the multi-pool scaling-up design approach and inline production of ammonium sulfate crystals. A 3-pool VaSA prototype was operated with anaerobically digested sludge at a municipal Water Resource Recovery Facility to recover ammonia and optimize its design. It was then operated with anaerobically digested dairy manure at a dairy farm to effectively produce ammonium sulfate crystals. The crystals can be marketed as high purity (99% ammonium sulfate) nitrogen fertilizer or reagent-grade chemical. The second objective of this project was to validate the feasibility and evaluate the benefits of integrating VaSA into anaerobic digestion systems. When ammonia is accumulated in digesters, biomethane production by anaerobic digestion of sludge and animal manure is suppressed. To avoid ammonia inhibition to methane-producing microorganisms, digestate may be withdrawn and, after ammonia recovery, returned to digesters. For the first time, this project found that up to 25% of the digestate can be replaced per day with VaSA-treated digestate while maintaining stable methane production in anaerobic digesters under thermo-alkaline conditions at an organic loading rate as high as 6.5-7.0 g-volatile solids/L-reactor/d.

The VaSA technology holds a great potential to be the 1st scalable innovation that promotes the shift of wastewater treatment paradigm from costly ammonia removal to profitable ammonia recovery. Energy consumption by VaSA is moderate because of the lower boiling point under vacuum and vacuum supply costs minor. Compared with conventional biological nitrogen removal, VaSA substantially reduces operational costs for water resource recovery facilities to meet discharge permit limits and reduce manure transportation costs for concentrated animal feeding operations to apply more low-ammonia manure on nearby land. The recovered fertilizers and upgraded biosolids and manure solids generate revenues for the facilities and operations. Converting ammonia in waste streams into ammonium fertilizers is a sustainable alternative to the energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis and nitrogen fertilizer manufacture. When VaSA is coupled with anaerobic digestion, digesters can treat greater amounts of wastes, produce more renewable natural gas, and upgrade biosolids and animal manure.
